passages.text: For more than two decades, India's information technology industry built something genuinely admirable: a world class services engine that became the back office of the global economy. TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCL Tech, and Tech Mahindra collectively generated hundreds of billions of dollars in revenue, employed millions of engineers, and powered an entire ecosystem of technical education across the country. Then came the AI revolution - and the industry was caught almost entirely unprepared. The launch of ChatGPT in November 2022 was not a sudden shock. It was the visible peak of a transformation building since deep learning went mainstream after 2015. But Indian IT firms, locked into low-risk service contracts and investing less than three per cent of revenues in R&D compared to ten to twenty per cent at global technology companies, had neither the incentive nor the institutional culture to see it coming. By the time the alarm was impossible to ignore, the frontier had already been claimed by OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, Meta, and a set of well-funded Chinese laboratories. What followed was a period of genuine reckoning. The traditional pyramid model, in which armies of junior engineers churned out standardised code with revenues scaling directly with headcount, began to crack. AI could now perform many of those base layer tasks: routine code generation, testing, data processing, and documentation. At the same time, the growth of over 2,000 Global Capability Centres meant multinationals that once outsourced wholesale were now building substantial in-house teams in India. The existential question became unavoidable: if Indian IT cannot build the AI, and its traditional clients are increasingly building their own teams, what exactly is the industry's role? Four structural failures explain why Indian IT missed the frontier AI race entirely. The first is the services trap. (Source:The Statesman)

passages.text: Feeling depressed about the state of the world? Worried about the future? You're not alone. Pessimism about politics is the new normal among the peoples of the west. Major conflicts in Europe and the Middle East and the harms caused by right-left extremism, stagnating economies, inequality, corruption, terrorism, racism, big tech, mass extinctions and the climate crisis make for shared nightmares. Growing numbers of people simply refuse to personally engage with current events via the news media, finding them too anxiety-inducing (so they probably won't be reading this). In a Reuters Institute survey last year, 40% of respondents in about 50 countries said they sometimes or often avoid the news altogether, a rise of 29% on 2017. Intense negativity characterises European and, to a lesser degree, North American political sentiment. In France, 90% of people questioned by Ipsos believed their country is on the wrong track. In Britain, it was 79%; in Germany, 77%; in the US, 60%. Europeans feel similarly glum about the bigger, global picture, unlike the Chinese, Saudis and Nigerians who are broadly upbeat, according to a GlobeScan survey. Pew Research Center polling in 25 countries last year found that the US, Russia and China are seen, by most but not all, as the biggest international threats. For Turks, for example, Israel is the main menace; for Greeks, it's the Turks. It gets more confusing still. Canada is one of several countries in which majorities regard the US as both the main threat and main ally. Disenchantment with democracy and dissatisfaction with political leaders is a ubiquitous, polarising western phenomenon. Divisions grow entrenched. Keir Starmer, with a 27% approval rating, according to Statista, is struggling to survive. Yet Germany's chancellor, Friedrich Merz, and France's president, Emmanuel Macron, are even less popular, on 19% and 18% respectively. Donald Trump is down to about 38% approval, trailing his nemesis, Canada's prime minister, Mark Carney, on 54%. In Russia, Vladimir Putin's historically inflated ratings are now badly punctured. Figures for Xi Jinping are unreliable; in China, freely expressing opinions is dangerous. India is an exception. A majority frankly adores the prime minister, Narendra Modi. (Source: The Gurdian)

passages.text: Recent diplomatic tensions between the United States and Iran have intensified after Iran responded to a U.S.-backed peace proposal with conditions that Washington has described as "unacceptable." The proposal, aimed at ending ongoing conflict and stabilizing the region, includes major demands such as lifting sanctions, a structured 30-day negotiation period, and nuclear-related concessions. However, Iran's counter-response has created fresh disagreements over the terms of peace and the future of regional security. At the centre of the dispute is Iran's demand for complete lifting of U.S. sanctions and unfreezing of Iranian assets abroad. Iran has also insisted on an end to military pressure, including naval restrictions and blockades affecting key trade routes like the Strait of Hormuz. In return, Iran has offered a phased approach to negotiations, suggesting that key issues, including nuclear concerns, could be resolved within a 30-day framework. However, it has refused to dismantle its nuclear infrastructure, which remains a major point of conflict with the U.S. proposal. The United States, on the other hand, has pushed for stricter conditions. These include long-term limits on uranium enrichment, removal of highly enriched uranium stockpiles, and strong verification measures. American officials argue that Iran's proposals do not go far enough to guarantee regional stability or prevent future escalation. Former President Donald Trump, who is closely associated with the negotiations, publicly rejected Iran's response, calling it "totally unacceptable" and warning of possible renewed military action if no agreement is reached. The situation has also impacted global markets and geopolitical stability. Oil prices have fluctuated due to uncertainty over the Strait of Hormuz, a vital energy route. Meanwhile, diplomatic mediators, including Pakistan, are attempting to bridge the gap between both sides. In conclusion, the Iran-US negotiations highlight deep mistrust and conflicting expectations. While both sides express willingness to negotiate, differences over sanctions, nuclear policy, and regional control continue to block progress toward a lasting peace agreement. (Source: The telegraph)

passages.text: India's mental health crisis is both vast and underappreciated. According to the Global Burden of Disease study, nearly 197 million Indians - roughly one in seven - live with some form of mental disorder. Depression and anxiety alone affect over 90 million people, yet for most, professional support remains out of reach. For decades, stigma was considered the primary barrier. By 2025, however, the conversation had shifted. Stigma, while still present, was no longer the central obstacle. The more urgent questions had become practical ones: how does care actually function once someone seeks help, and what happens when symptoms escalate? The answer, increasingly, lies in integrated, end-to-end models of care. India's mental health systems were historically built around isolated touchpoints - therapy sessions existed separately from psychiatric care, digital tools operated independently of clinical oversight, and hospitalisation sat at the extreme end of the spectrum, disconnected from what came before and after. Individuals and families were expected to navigate these transitions alone, often during periods of acute vulnerability. Effective systems, experts argue, must allow individuals to move fluidly between levels of support - digital guidance, outpatient care, crisis intervention, and structured inpatient settings - without losing continuity of care. Technology has played a critical role in widening access. The government's Tele-MANAS platform, upgraded in 2025 with a multilingual interface in ten regional languages and an AI-powered chatbot named Asmi, has expanded mental health outreach significantly. Private platforms such as Wysa, Amaha, and Lissun are using AI-driven tools to reach underserved populations. However, a key lesson from 2025 is that access alone is insufficient. Digital tools can open doors, but they cannot substitute for trained professionals or structured clinical care. Looking ahead, India's mental healthcare challenge in 2026 is one of consolidation rather than experimentation. Hospitals, outpatient centres, digital platforms, workplaces, and community networks must function as parts of a coherent whole. Equally important is recognising families not merely as informal caregivers but as active stakeholders in recovery. The opportunity is significant - India has the chance to build a mental healthcare system that is preventative, responsive, and continuous, one that meets people where they are. (Source: National Mental Health Survey of India)

passages.text: Philosophy in the Upaniṣads does not merely consist of abstract claims about the nature of reality, but is also presented as a way of living one's life. In Yājñavalkya's teaching to Janaka, for example, knowledge of atman is associated with a change in one's disposition and behavior. As we have seen, karma is characterized as a natural moral process, with knowledge of the self as a way out of that process. In this respect, a fundamental assumption throughout many teachings of the self is that it is untouched by karma. Yajñavalkya teaches Janaka that knowledge of the self is beyond virtuous (kalyana) and evil (papa)-that, through knowledge of the self one reaches the world of brahman, where the good or bad actions of one's life do not follow. Yajñavalkya explains that in the world of brahman a thief is not a thief, a murderer is not a murderer, an outcaste not an outcaste, a mixed- caste person (paulkasa) is not a mixed-caste person, a renunciate (sramana) is not a renunciate, and an ascetic not an ascetic, that neither the good (punya) nor the evil (papa) follow him. In using these examples Yajñavalkya illustrates the degree to which knowledge of the self is beyond everyday notions of moral behavior. In other words, he seems to be saying that even if one has committed evil deeds, one can still be liberated from karma by means of knowing the self. Yet Yajñavalkya is not suggesting that one can continue to perform 'evil' deeds without suffering karmic retribution. Rather, as he asserts later in his discussion with Janaka: when one is knowledgeable, one necessarily acts morally. Yajñavalkya explains that a man who has proper knowledge becomes calm (santa), restrained (danta), withdrawn (uparata), patient (titiksu), and composed (samaahita). Here Yajñavalkya characterizes knowledge of the self as a change in one's disposition. In other words, one who is a knower of the self becomes a person of good character and-by definition-would not perform an evil action. While Yajñavalkya talks about becoming calm, restrained, withdrawn, patient, and composed, these dispositions are not presented as virtues to cultivate for the sake of knowledge, but rather as consequences of knowing atman. Subsequent texts would devote considerable attention to how one should cultivate oneself in order to achieve the highest knowledge. For example, both the eight-fold path of the Buddhist Nikayas and the eight limbs in the Yoga Sutra suggest that one needs to live a moral life in order to achieve true knowledge. In Yajñavalkya's teaching about atman, however, there is more attention paid to the objective of knowing the self than the ethical means of controlling the self. (Source: https://iep.utm.edu/upanisad)

passages.text: Mission Drishti, the world's first OptoSAR satellite developed by Bengaluru based space startup GalaxEye has been successfully launched on May 3, 2026 aboard a Falcon 9 by SpaceX from Vandenberg, California. Weighing 190 kilograms, Mission Drishti is India's largest privately developed Earth observation satellite. "It is the first satellite globally to integrate Electro-Optical (EO) and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) sensors into a single operational platform, enabling all-weather, day-and-night imaging capabilities. This integrated approach addresses long-standing limitations of conventional systems and enables more reliable and consistent data acquisition across diverse environmental conditions," GalaxEye said. "Mission Drishti marks our first mission and the culmination of over five years of sustained R&D to develop this breakthrough technology. With the satellite now successfully in orbit, our immediate focus is on completing its commissioning. As we move through this phase, we are already witnessing strong global interest in the differentiated datasets enabled by our OptoSAR payload." said Suyash Singh, Founder & CEO, GalaxEye. Following its successful deployment and commissioning initial imagery is expected to be delivered to customers in the coming weeks. GalaxEye said that the satellite has already generated significant interest from government and commercial stakeholders internationally, seeking access to high-quality, high-frequency Earth observation data. On the successful launch, Dr. Pawan Goenka, Chairman, Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Center (IN-SPACe) said that the sustained effort over the last five to six years on confidence-building, capacity-building and the commercialisation of India's private space technology ecosystem is now showing tangible results. "Mission Drishti by GalaxEye is a fine example of this - the world's first OptoSAR satellite from an Indian private player. As more Indian space companies demonstrate their capabilities through real missions and engagement with global customers, confidence in India's space ecosystem will continue to strengthen, creating greater demand both in India and overseas. I compliment the GalaxEye team on this important milestone and wish them continued success," said Dr. Goenka. Mission Drishti is a dual-use Earth observation Satellite, supporting use cases across defence, agriculture, disaster management, maritime monitoring, and infrastructure planning. The satellite is expected to complement India's broader initiatives, including the active 29 Earth Observation satellites outlined in ISRO's recent annual report.

passages.text: Prime Minister Narendra Modi has made an appeal that has the entire nation talking. To put it crudely, he said: "don't buy gold for a year; postpone foreign travel; work from home where possible." His message is simple: Save dollars, protect India's foreign exchange reserves. His appeal comes amid the ongoing Iran war, and the resultant rise in crude oil prices, and pressure on the rupee. But how exactly does skipping gold purchases help India's forex position? The answer lies in the math. India's forex reserves are around $690.69 billion, according to data compiled by Trading Economics. RBI data shows reserves rising close to $728 billion in February before slipping back to around $691 billion in April as global uncertainty intensified. At the same time, the IMF has projected that India's current account deficit (CAD) could widen to $84.5 billion in 2026, roughly 2 per cent of GDP. A widening CAD means one thing: more dollars going out than coming in. And gold is a big reason for that. India imported about $72 billion worth of gold in FY26 -- this is a 24 per cent jump from the previous year. In fact, India is the world's second-largest gold buyer. Most of this gold is imported. And every ounce is paid for in dollars.

passages.text: International Humanitarian Law (IHL), also referred to as the law of armed conflict or the law of war, consists of rules intended to limit the effects of armed conflict for humanitarian reasons. Rather than determining whether a war itself is lawful, IHL regulates conduct during armed conflict and seeks to balance military necessity with humanitarian considerations. Its primary objectives are to protect persons who are not, or are no longer, participating in hostilities and to restrict methods and means of warfare that cause unnecessary suffering. IHL principally applies during international and non-international armed conflicts. Among its most fundamental principles is the principle of distinction, which requires parties to a conflict to distinguish at all times between civilians and combatants, and between civilian objects and military objectives. Attacks may lawfully be directed only against military objectives. Civilian persons and civilian objects, such as schools, hospitals, and homes, cannot ordinarily be targeted merely because incidental military advantage may arise from their destruction. Closely related is the principle of proportionality, which prohibits attacks expected to cause incidental civilian harm that would be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated. This principle does not prohibit all civilian casualties; rather, it seeks to prevent disproportionate harm. Even where a legitimate military objective exists, military operations must not impose excessive burdens on civilians. The principle of military necessity permits only those measures necessary to achieve a legitimate military objective and not otherwise prohibited by international law. However, military necessity does not override all humanitarian obligations. Certain weapons and practices remain prohibited because they cause unnecessary suffering or fail to distinguish between military and civilian targets. Thus, military convenience cannot justify every action during war. Another important principle is humanity, which prohibits means and methods of warfare causing superfluous injury or unnecessary suffering. Torture, cruel treatment, collective punishment, and attacks directed primarily to spread terror among civilians are generally prohibited. Persons who are wounded, detained, or otherwise hors de combat (out of combat) are entitled to humane treatment irrespective of nationality or allegiance. The law also recognises the protection of medical personnel and humanitarian workers. Hospitals and medical units generally enjoy special protection because they serve humanitarian functions. However, such protection may cease if these facilities are used, outside their humanitarian purpose, for acts harmful to the enemy, though reasonable warning may be required before protection is withdrawn. Violations of serious IHL obligations may amount to war crimes. However, superior orders do not automatically excuse unlawful conduct. Individuals may bear responsibility where they knowingly participate in grave violations of humanitarian norms.

passages.text: Constitutional democracies ordinarily distribute governmental authority among different institutions to prevent concentration of power in a single body. This arrangement is reflected in the doctrine of separation of powers, under which legislative bodies generally enact laws, the executive implements and administers them, and the judiciary interprets and applies them. The doctrine does not necessarily require a rigid or absolute division of functions. Modern constitutional systems often permit a degree of overlap because complete separation may be impractical. Nevertheless, the central purpose remains to ensure checks and balances so that no organ exercises uncontrolled power. One of the most significant constitutional mechanisms preserving this balance is judicial review. Judicial review refers to the power of courts to examine the validity of legislative enactments and executive actions and determine whether they conform to constitutional requirements. Courts exercising judicial review do not ordinarily assess whether a law is wise, economically beneficial, or politically desirable. Rather, they examine whether constitutional limitations have been violated. Thus, disagreement with legislative policy is distinct from constitutional invalidity. At the same time, courts generally recognise that elected branches possess institutional competence in certain areas involving policy decisions, economic regulation, allocation of resources, and matters requiring specialised expertise. Therefore, judicial restraint is sometimes considered appropriate where constitutional rights are not directly threatened. However, judicial restraint does not imply judicial abdication. Courts may intervene where governmental actions are arbitrary, violate constitutional guarantees, exceed legal authority, or undermine fundamental rights. The doctrine of checks and balances recognises that constitutional organs may possess limited powers to review or influence one another. Such interaction does not necessarily destroy separation of powers. For instance, executive actions may require legislative approval, legislation may be subject to constitutional scrutiny by courts, and certain appointments or actions may involve more than one branch. Constitutional governance therefore involves both separation and controlled interaction. Another important constitutional principle is the rule of law, which requires that governmental power be exercised according to established legal principles rather than personal discretion or arbitrary preference. Under the rule of law, all individuals and institutions, including public authorities, remain accountable to law. Arbitrary exercises of power are inconsistent with constitutional governance because they undermine predictability, equality, and fairness. Constitutional adjudication also frequently involves balancing majoritarian decision-making and constitutional rights. Democratic institutions ordinarily function according to majority preference. However, constitutional systems recognise that majoritarian support alone cannot justify actions violating fundamental rights. Constitutional guarantees often exist precisely to protect individuals and minority groups from excessive exercises of governmental power.

passages.text: A contract of guarantee is a contract to perform the promise or discharge the liability of a third person in case of his default. It ordinarily involves three parties: the principal debtor, who is primarily liable for the debt or obligation; the creditor, to whom the obligation is owed; and the surety, who undertakes to discharge the liability if the principal debtor fails to do so. The liability of the surety is generally co- extensive with that of the principal debtor, unless otherwise provided by the contract. This means that the surety may be called upon to satisfy the same obligation that the principal debtor was bound to perform. Unlike ordinary contracts, consideration in a contract of guarantee may consist of any act, promise, or benefit done for the benefit of the principal debtor. It is not necessary that the surety receive direct consideration personally. However, a valid guarantee requires free consent, and if consent is obtained through misrepresentation or concealment of material facts, the guarantee may become invalid. For instance, if the creditor deliberately suppresses information regarding the financial condition or conduct of the principal debtor and such information would have influenced the surety's decision, the guarantee may be affected. Guarantees may be specific or continuing. A specific guarantee applies to a single transaction or obligation and comes to an end once that transaction is completed. A continuing guarantee, however, extends to a series of transactions and remains operative until revoked or otherwise terminated according to law. A continuing guarantee may be revoked by the surety concerning future transactions through notice to the creditor. However, such revocation does not affect transactions that have already occurred before the notice was given. Further, the death of a surety ordinarily operates as revocation of a continuing guarantee with respect to future transactions, unless there exists a contract providing otherwise. The law also recognises certain circumstances under which the surety may be discharged from liability. A surety may be discharged if the creditor and principal debtor enter into a contract varying the terms of the original agreement without the surety's consent, where the creditor releases the principal debtor, or where the creditor acts in a manner impairing the surety's eventual remedies against the principal debtor. Such discharge may occur because the surety agreed to guarantee only a specific obligation and should not be subjected to materially altered risks without consent. After satisfying the debt, the surety acquires certain rights against the principal debtor. This principle, often referred to as subrogation, permits the surety to step into the shoes of the creditor and exercise the rights that the creditor could have exercised against the principal debtor. The surety may also claim indemnification from the principal debtor for amounts rightfully paid under the guarantee.

passages.text: The law of tort recognises that a person may not always be held liable for damage merely because harm has occurred. Certain circumstances may excuse liability where the defendant demonstrates that the event occurred despite the exercise of reasonable care and caution. Two closely related yet distinct concepts in this regard are inevitable accident and Act of God (Vis Major). Although both may relieve a defendant from liability, they differ in their origin and legal requirements. An inevitable accident refers to an occurrence which could not have been prevented despite the exercise of reasonable care, caution, and skill by the defendant. The central inquiry is not whether the event caused damage, but whether a reasonable and prudent person exercising ordinary care could have avoided it. The event may arise from human conduct, mechanical failure, or unforeseen circumstances. However, the defendant cannot rely upon inevitable accident where negligence, omission, or lack of proper precautions contributed to the occurrence. Thus, a person who fails to inspect equipment, ignores warning signs, or neglects ordinary safety measures cannot later claim that the accident was inevitable. An Act of God, on the other hand, is a natural event arising exclusively from forces of nature that are so extraordinary and unforeseeable that no amount of human foresight or reasonable care could prevent the resulting damage. Examples may include unprecedented floods, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, or violent natural disturbances. The natural event must operate independently of human intervention and must be so unusual that it could not reasonably have been anticipated. Ordinary seasonal rainfall, predictable weather conditions, or recurring natural events generally do not qualify merely because they cause harm. The distinction between these principles becomes important where natural events and human conduct combine. If a natural event merely contributes to the damage but human negligence substantially contributes to the loss, liability may still arise. Conversely, where the defendant exercised reasonable care and the damage was solely attributable to an extraordinary natural force, the defence of Act of God may succeed. The burden generally lies upon the defendant to establish facts supporting these defences. Further, where a defendant voluntarily undertakes a hazardous activity or introduces potentially dangerous things into their control, courts may closely examine whether reasonable precautions proportionate to the risk were adopted.

passages.text: Criminal liability generally arises where an individual directly commits an offence. However, the law also recognises that a person may be held responsible even without personally carrying out the prohibited act. This principle is reflected in the law relating to abetment, which seeks to punish conduct encouraging, facilitating, or assisting the commission of an offence. The rationale is that a person who deliberately contributes to the commission of an offence may be as blameworthy as the person physically committing it. Abetment may arise in three principal ways: instigation, conspiracy, and intentional aiding. Though these concepts may overlap in certain situations, they are distinct in their legal requirements. Instigation refers to actively provoking, urging, inciting, encouraging, or stimulating another person to commit an act. Such encouragement may be express or implied and may occur through words, conduct, written communication, or even deliberate omission in certain circumstances. However, mere casual remarks, expressions of anger, or statements lacking intention to provoke commission of an offence may not amount to instigation. The focus lies upon whether the accused intended to influence or encourage another person toward committing the act. Abetment by conspiracy occurs where two or more persons agree to commit an unlawful act or agree to commit a lawful act through unlawful means, and some act or illegal omission takes place in furtherance of that agreement. Mere knowledge of an unlawful plan or passive association with conspirators does not by itself constitute conspiracy. There must ordinarily exist a meeting of minds and some step taken toward execution of the common design. Abetment by intentional aiding occurs where a person intentionally facilitates commission of an offence through acts or omissions. Aid may take various forms, including providing tools, information, transport, shelter, or any other assistance that substantially contributes to the offence. Mere presence at the scene of occurrence does not necessarily amount to aiding unless accompanied by conduct intended to facilitate commission of the offence. A person may be liable for abetment even if the principal offence ultimately differs in manner from what was originally intended, provided the consequences are a probable result of the conduct encouraged or assisted. However, where the principal offender acts independently and outside the scope of what was instigated or facilitated, liability for abetment may not arise.

passages.text: A rapidly growing food delivery company, QuickBasket, had recently expanded its services to several smaller cities. Although customer orders increased significantly, the company soon began facing complaints regarding delayed deliveries, incorrect orders, and poor customer support. Employees working in different city offices also reported confusion about delivery procedures and inconsistent instructions from managers. Concerned that these issues could damage the company's reputation, the board appointed an operations consultant to study the organization and recommend solutions. The consultant interacted with senior managers, delivery executives, customer support staff, restaurant partners, and customers to understand the problems more clearly. After reviewing delivery records, customer complaints, and employee feedback, the consultant found that different regional offices were following separate systems for assigning orders and tracking deliveries. Many delivery executives had also not received proper training in handling customer complaints or using the company's updated mobile application efficiently. To improve operations, the consultant suggested introducing a unified digital tracking system across all branches, conducting training workshops for employees, and creating a centralized customer support department to respond to complaints more quickly. However, some regional managers opposed the reforms because they believed that a common system would reduce their control over local operations. To address these concerns, the consultant organized meetings with managers, explained the long-term benefits of coordination, and encouraged employees to provide suggestions before changes were implemented. The overall objective was to create a more efficient, customer-friendly, and coordinated organization capable of maintaining growth in a competitive market.

passages.text: Twelve friends attended a cultural fest. Six of them - A, B, C, D, E, and F - are seated in a row facing North, while the other six - G, H, I, J, K, and L - are seated in another row facing South, though not necessarily in the same order. Each person in one row faces exactly one person in the other row. Each friend prefers a different beverage - Coffee, Tea, Lemon Juice, Mango Shake, Lassi, Coconut Water, Cold Coffee, Buttermilk, Green Tea, Orange Juice, Milkshake, and Soda. questions.passageText: For more than two decades, India's information technology industry built something genuinely admirable: a world class services engine that became the back office of the global economy. TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCL Tech, and Tech Mahindra collectively generated hundreds of billions of dollars in revenue, employed millions of engineers, and powered an entire ecosystem of technical education across the country. Then came the AI revolution - and the industry was caught almost entirely unprepared. The launch of ChatGPT in November 2022 was not a sudden shock. It was the visible peak of a transformation building since deep learning went mainstream after 2015. But Indian IT firms, locked into low-risk service contracts and investing less than three per cent of revenues in R&D compared to ten to twenty per cent at global technology companies, had neither the incentive nor the institutional culture to see it coming. By the time the alarm was impossible to ignore, the frontier had already been claimed by OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, Meta, and a set of well-funded Chinese laboratories. What followed was a period of genuine reckoning. The traditional pyramid model, in which armies of junior engineers churned out standardised code with revenues scaling directly with headcount, began to crack. AI could now perform many of those base layer tasks: routine code generation, testing, data processing, and documentation. At the same time, the growth of over 2,000 Global Capability Centres meant multinationals that once outsourced wholesale were now building substantial in-house teams in India. The existential question became unavoidable: if Indian IT cannot build the AI, and its traditional clients are increasingly building their own teams, what exactly is the industry's role? Four structural failures explain why Indian IT missed the frontier AI race entirely. The first is the services trap. (Source:The Statesman)
options: Indian IT firms built a globally respected services base but underestimated how quickly multinational clients would reduce dependence on outsourced work.
Indian IT firms created a powerful services-led industry but failed to prepare for the AI-driven disruption of their own operating model.
Indian IT firms became major global vendors but could not match frontier laboratories because they lacked a culture of original product innovation.
Indian IT firms expanded technical employment at scale but remained exposed when global technology companies moved ahead in applied AI research.
questions.solution: Official source answer key: Choice B.

questions.passageText: Feeling depressed about the state of the world? Worried about the future? You're not alone. Pessimism about politics is the new normal among the peoples of the west. Major conflicts in Europe and the Middle East and the harms caused by right-left extremism, stagnating economies, inequality, corruption, terrorism, racism, big tech, mass extinctions and the climate crisis make for shared nightmares. Growing numbers of people simply refuse to personally engage with current events via the news media, finding them too anxiety-inducing (so they probably won't be reading this). In a Reuters Institute survey last year, 40% of respondents in about 50 countries said they sometimes or often avoid the news altogether, a rise of 29% on 2017. Intense negativity characterises European and, to a lesser degree, North American political sentiment. In France, 90% of people questioned by Ipsos believed their country is on the wrong track. In Britain, it was 79%; in Germany, 77%; in the US, 60%. Europeans feel similarly glum about the bigger, global picture, unlike the Chinese, Saudis and Nigerians who are broadly upbeat, according to a GlobeScan survey. Pew Research Center polling in 25 countries last year found that the US, Russia and China are seen, by most but not all, as the biggest international threats. For Turks, for example, Israel is the main menace; for Greeks, it's the Turks. It gets more confusing still. Canada is one of several countries in which majorities regard the US as both the main threat and main ally. Disenchantment with democracy and dissatisfaction with political leaders is a ubiquitous, polarising western phenomenon. Divisions grow entrenched. Keir Starmer, with a 27% approval rating, according to Statista, is struggling to survive. Yet Germany's chancellor, Friedrich Merz, and France's president, Emmanuel Macron, are even less popular, on 19% and 18% respectively. Donald Trump is down to about 38% approval, trailing his nemesis, Canada's prime minister, Mark Carney, on 54%. In Russia, Vladimir Putin's historically inflated ratings are now badly punctured. Figures for Xi Jinping are unreliable; in China, freely expressing opinions is dangerous. India is an exception. A majority frankly adores the prime minister, Narendra Modi. (Source: The Gurdian)
options: Western publics are increasingly pessimistic about politics, global crises, and leadership, even as some non-Western societies remain comparatively hopeful.
Western publics are avoiding political news mainly because media coverage exaggerates global crises, leadership failures, and democratic instability.
Western publics are losing trust in democracy because rival powers such as China, Russia, and the US are viewed as equal threats.
Western publics are politically divided because unpopular leaders have failed to address extremism, climate change, corruption, and economic inequality.
questions.solution: Official source answer key: Choice A.

questions.passageText: Recent diplomatic tensions between the United States and Iran have intensified after Iran responded to a U.S.-backed peace proposal with conditions that Washington has described as "unacceptable." The proposal, aimed at ending ongoing conflict and stabilizing the region, includes major demands such as lifting sanctions, a structured 30-day negotiation period, and nuclear-related concessions. However, Iran's counter-response has created fresh disagreements over the terms of peace and the future of regional security. At the centre of the dispute is Iran's demand for complete lifting of U.S. sanctions and unfreezing of Iranian assets abroad. Iran has also insisted on an end to military pressure, including naval restrictions and blockades affecting key trade routes like the Strait of Hormuz. In return, Iran has offered a phased approach to negotiations, suggesting that key issues, including nuclear concerns, could be resolved within a 30-day framework. However, it has refused to dismantle its nuclear infrastructure, which remains a major point of conflict with the U.S. proposal. The United States, on the other hand, has pushed for stricter conditions. These include long-term limits on uranium enrichment, removal of highly enriched uranium stockpiles, and strong verification measures. American officials argue that Iran's proposals do not go far enough to guarantee regional stability or prevent future escalation. Former President Donald Trump, who is closely associated with the negotiations, publicly rejected Iran's response, calling it "totally unacceptable" and warning of possible renewed military action if no agreement is reached. The situation has also impacted global markets and geopolitical stability. Oil prices have fluctuated due to uncertainty over the Strait of Hormuz, a vital energy route. questions.passageText: India's mental health crisis is both vast and underappreciated. According to the Global Burden of Disease study, nearly 197 million Indians - roughly one in seven - live with some form of mental disorder. Depression and anxiety alone affect over 90 million people, yet for most, professional support remains out of reach. For decades, stigma was considered the primary barrier. By 2025, however, the conversation had shifted. Stigma, while still present, was no longer the central obstacle. The more urgent questions had become practical ones: how does care actually function once someone seeks help, and what happens when symptoms escalate? The answer, increasingly, lies in integrated, end-to-end models of care. India's mental health systems were historically built around isolated touchpoints - therapy sessions existed separately from psychiatric care, digital tools operated independently of clinical oversight, and hospitalisation sat at the extreme end of the spectrum, disconnected from what came before and after. Individuals and families were expected to navigate these transitions alone, often during periods of acute vulnerability. Effective systems, experts argue, must allow individuals to move fluidly between levels of support - digital guidance, outpatient care, crisis intervention, and structured inpatient settings - without losing continuity of care. Technology has played a critical role in widening access. The government's Tele-MANAS platform, upgraded in 2025 with a multilingual interface in ten regional languages and an AI-powered chatbot named Asmi, has expanded mental health outreach significantly. Private platforms such as Wysa, Amaha, and Lissun are using AI-driven tools to reach underserved populations. However, a key lesson from 2025 is that access alone is insufficient. Digital tools can open doors, but they cannot substitute for trained professionals or structured clinical care. Looking ahead, India's mental healthcare challenge in 2026 is one of consolidation rather than experimentation. Hospitals, outpatient centres, digital platforms, workplaces, and community networks must function as parts of a coherent whole. Equally important is recognising families not merely as informal caregivers but as active stakeholders in recovery. The opportunity is significant - India has the chance to build a mental healthcare system that is preventative, responsive, and continuous, one that meets people where they are. (Source: National Mental Health Survey of India)

The government's investment in Tele-MANAS and NIMHANS has made India's mental health infrastructure globally competitive.
Digital technology and AI-powered platforms have largely resolved India's mental health crisis by making care widely accessible.

questions.passageText: Philosophy in the Upaniṣads does not merely consist of abstract claims about the nature of reality, but is also presented as a way of living one's life. In Yājñavalkya's teaching to Janaka, for example, knowledge of atman is associated with a change in one's disposition and behavior. As we have seen, karma is characterized as a natural moral process, with knowledge of the self as a way out of that process. In this respect, a fundamental assumption throughout many teachings of the self is that it is untouched by karma. Yajñavalkya teaches Janaka that knowledge of the self is beyond virtuous (kalyana) and evil (papa)-that, through knowledge of the self one reaches the world of brahman, where the good or bad actions of one's life do not follow. Yajñavalkya explains that in the world of brahman a thief is not a thief, a murderer is not a murderer, an outcaste not an outcaste, a mixed- caste person (paulkasa) is not a mixed-caste person, a renunciate (sramana) is not a renunciate, and an ascetic not an ascetic, that neither the good (punya) nor the evil (papa) follow him. In using these examples Yajñavalkya illustrates the degree to which knowledge of the self is beyond everyday notions of moral behavior. In other words, he seems to be saying that even if one has committed evil deeds, one can still be liberated from karma by means of knowing the self. Yet Yajñavalkya is not suggesting that one can continue to perform 'evil' deeds without suffering karmic retribution. Rather, as he asserts later in his discussion with Janaka: when one is knowledgeable, one necessarily acts morally. Yajñavalkya explains that a man who has proper knowledge becomes calm (santa), restrained (danta), withdrawn (uparata), patient (titiksu), and composed (samaahita). Here Yajñavalkya characterizes knowledge of the self as a change in one's disposition. In other words, one who is a knower of the self becomes a person of good character and-by definition-would not perform an evil action. While Yajñavalkya talks about becoming calm, restrained, withdrawn, patient, and composed, these dispositions are not presented as virtues to cultivate for the sake of knowledge, but rather as consequences of knowing atman. Subsequent texts would devote considerable attention to how one should cultivate oneself in order to achieve the highest knowledge. For example, both the eight-fold path of the Buddhist Nikayas and the eight limbs in the Yoga Sutra suggest that one needs to live a moral life in order to achieve true knowledge. In Yajñavalkya's teaching about atman, however, there is more attention paid to the objective of knowing the self than the ethical means of controlling the self. (Source: https://iep.utm.edu/upanisad)
options: Knowledge of the self enables one to transcend the effects of karma.
A knowledgeable person naturally develops morally disciplined conduct.
The Upaniṣads emphasise moral discipline before attaining self-knowledge.
Buddhist and Yogic traditions emphasise ethics before spiritual knowledge.
questions.solution: Official source answer key: Choice C.

questions.passageText: Mission Drishti, the world's first OptoSAR satellite developed by Bengaluru based space startup GalaxEye has been successfully launched on May 3, 2026 aboard a Falcon 9 by SpaceX from Vandenberg, California. Weighing 190 kilograms, Mission Drishti is India's largest privately developed Earth observation satellite. "It is the first satellite globally to integrate Electro-Optical (EO) and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) sensors into a single operational platform, enabling all-weather, day-and-night imaging capabilities. This integrated approach addresses long-standing limitations of conventional systems and enables more reliable and consistent data acquisition across diverse environmental conditions," GalaxEye said. "Mission Drishti marks our first mission and the culmination of over five years of sustained R&D to develop this breakthrough technology. With the satellite now successfully in orbit, our immediate focus is on completing its commissioning. As we move through this phase, we are already witnessing strong global interest in the differentiated datasets enabled by our OptoSAR payload." said Suyash Singh, Founder & CEO, GalaxEye. Following its successful deployment and commissioning initial imagery is expected to be delivered to customers in the coming weeks. GalaxEye said that the satellite has already generated significant interest from government and commercial stakeholders internationally, seeking access to high-quality, high-frequency Earth observation data. On the successful launch, Dr. Pawan Goenka, Chairman, Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Center (IN-SPACe) said that the sustained effort over the last five to six years on confidence-building, capacity-building and the commercialisation of India's private space technology ecosystem is now showing tangible results. "Mission Drishti by GalaxEye is a fine example of this - the world's first OptoSAR satellite from an Indian private player. As more Indian space companies demonstrate their capabilities through real missions and engagement with global customers, confidence in India's space ecosystem will continue to strengthen, creating greater demand both in India and overseas. I compliment the GalaxEye team on this important milestone and wish them continued success," said Dr. Goenka. Mission Drishti is a dual-use Earth observation Satellite, supporting use cases across defence, agriculture, disaster management, maritime monitoring, and infrastructure planning. The satellite is expected to complement India's broader initiatives, including the active 29 Earth Observation satellites outlined in ISRO's recent annual report.

questions.questionText: During an armed conflict, State X receives credible intelligence that enemy forces have repeatedly used the rooftop of a functioning school over three consecutive days to relay troop coordinates. The school's lower floors continue to be used by approximately 200 students and remain in regular operation. The school is located near an active front line. Acting on this intelligence but without conducting a proportionality assessment or issuing any civilian warning, State X launches sustained missile strikes that destroy the entire building during school hours, causing extensive civilian casualties. questions.passageText: International Humanitarian Law (IHL), also referred to as the law of armed conflict or the law of war, consists of rules intended to limit the effects of armed conflict for humanitarian reasons. Rather than determining whether a war itself is lawful, IHL regulates conduct during armed conflict and seeks to balance military necessity with humanitarian considerations. Its primary objectives are to protect persons who are not, or are no longer, participating in hostilities and to restrict methods and means of warfare that cause unnecessary suffering. IHL principally applies during international and non-international armed conflicts. Among its most fundamental principles is the principle of distinction, which requires parties to a conflict to distinguish at all times between civilians and combatants, and between civilian objects and military objectives. Attacks may lawfully be directed only against military objectives. Civilian persons and civilian objects, such as schools, hospitals, and homes, cannot ordinarily be targeted merely because incidental military advantage may arise from their destruction. Closely related is the principle of proportionality, which prohibits attacks expected to cause incidental civilian harm that would be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated. This principle does not prohibit all civilian casualties; rather, it seeks to prevent disproportionate harm. Even where a legitimate military objective exists, military operations must not impose excessive burdens on civilians. The principle of military necessity permits only those measures necessary to achieve a legitimate military objective and not otherwise prohibited by international law. However, military necessity does not override all humanitarian obligations. Certain weapons and practices remain prohibited because they cause unnecessary suffering or fail to distinguish between military and civilian targets. Thus, military convenience cannot justify every action during war. Another important principle is humanity, which prohibits means and methods of warfare causing superfluous injury or unnecessary suffering. Torture, cruel treatment, collective punishment, and attacks directed primarily to spread terror among civilians are generally prohibited. Persons who are wounded, detained, or otherwise hors de combat (out of combat) are entitled to humane treatment irrespective of nationality or allegiance. The law also recognises the protection of medical personnel and humanitarian workers. Hospitals and medical units generally enjoy special protection because they serve humanitarian functions. However, such protection may cease if these facilities are used, outside their humanitarian purpose, for acts harmful to the enemy, though reasonable warning may be required before protection is withdrawn. Violations of serious IHL obligations may amount to war crimes. However, superior orders do not automatically excuse unlawful conduct. Individuals may bear responsibility where they knowingly participate in grave violations of humanitarian norms.
options: The attack is lawful because credible, repeated military use of a structure by enemy forces is sufficient under IHL to classify it as a military objective, and the principle of military necessity permits its destruction irrespective of continued civilian occupation.

The attack is impermissible primarily because enemy forces occupied only the rooftop while students occupied the lower floors, meaning destruction of the entire building exceeded the scope of any legitimate military objective.

The attack may be permissible because military necessity allows commanders to act decisively on confirmed intelligence of repeated military use, and the school's proximity to an active front line further diminishes its ordinary civilian character.

The attack appears unlawful because targeting a building with substantial civilian occupancy through sustained strikes, without proportionality assessment or civilian warning, likely violates both the principle of distinction and the principle of proportionality.
questions.solution: Official source answer key: Choice D.

questions.passageText: International Humanitarian Law (IHL), also referred to as the law of armed conflict or the law of war, consists of rules intended to limit the effects of armed conflict for humanitarian reasons. Rather than determining whether a war itself is lawful, IHL regulates conduct during armed conflict and seeks to balance military necessity with humanitarian considerations. Its primary objectives are to protect persons who are not, or are no longer, participating in hostilities and to restrict methods and means of warfare that cause unnecessary suffering. IHL principally applies during international and non-international armed conflicts. Among its most fundamental principles is the principle of distinction, which requires parties to a conflict to distinguish at all times between civilians and combatants, and between civilian objects and military objectives. Attacks may lawfully be directed only against military objectives. Civilian persons and civilian objects, such as schools, hospitals, and homes, cannot ordinarily be targeted merely because incidental military advantage may arise from their destruction. Closely related is the principle of proportionality, which prohibits attacks expected to cause incidental civilian harm that would be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated. This principle does not prohibit all civilian casualties; rather, it seeks to prevent disproportionate harm. Even where a legitimate military objective exists, military operations must not impose excessive burdens on civilians. The principle of military necessity permits only those measures necessary to achieve a legitimate military objective and not otherwise prohibited by international law. However, military necessity does not override all humanitarian obligations. Certain weapons and practices remain prohibited because they cause unnecessary suffering or fail to distinguish between military and civilian targets. Thus, military convenience cannot justify every action during war. Another important principle is humanity, which prohibits means and methods of warfare causing superfluous injury or unnecessary suffering. Torture, cruel treatment, collective punishment, and attacks directed primarily to spread terror among civilians are generally prohibited. Persons who are wounded, detained, or otherwise hors de combat (out of combat) are entitled to humane treatment irrespective of nationality or allegiance. The law also recognises the protection of medical personnel and humanitarian workers. Hospitals and medical units generally enjoy special protection because they serve humanitarian functions. However, such protection may cease if these facilities are used, outside their humanitarian purpose, for acts harmful to the enemy, though reasonable warning may be required before protection is withdrawn. Violations of serious IHL obligations may amount to war crimes. However, superior orders do not automatically excuse unlawful conduct. Individuals may bear responsibility where they knowingly participate in grave violations of humanitarian norms.

The conduct is lawful because any measure increasing military success satisfies military necessity.

The conduct is permissible because IHL only protects civilians.

questions.questionText: The legislature of State X enacts a law requiring all print and digital news publications to submit content relating to public policy, national security, or electoral matters to a Government Media Review Board at least five days before publication. The Board is empowered to withhold approval if it determines the content poses a risk to 'social stability.' The government argues that the measure represents a legitimate exercise of legislative authority over media regulation, is supported by a large majority of citizens in opinion surveys, and that elected institutions are constitutionally competent to define permissible limits on public discourse. A petition challenging the law alleges violation of fundamental rights. Which of the following most appropriately follows from the passage?

questions.passageText: Constitutional democracies ordinarily distribute governmental authority among different institutions to prevent concentration of power in a single body. This arrangement is reflected in the doctrine of separation of powers, under which legislative bodies generally enact laws, the executive implements and administers them, and the judiciary interprets and applies them. The doctrine does not necessarily require a rigid or absolute division of functions. Modern constitutional systems often permit a degree of overlap because complete separation may be impractical. Nevertheless, the central purpose remains to ensure checks and balances so that no organ exercises uncontrolled power. One of the most significant constitutional mechanisms preserving this balance is judicial review. Judicial review refers to the power of courts to examine the validity of legislative enactments and executive actions and determine whether they conform to constitutional requirements. Courts exercising judicial review do not ordinarily assess whether a law is wise, economically beneficial, or politically desirable. Rather, they examine whether constitutional limitations have been violated. Thus, disagreement with legislative policy is distinct from constitutional invalidity. At the same time, courts generally recognise that elected branches possess institutional competence in certain areas involving policy decisions, economic regulation, allocation of resources, and matters requiring specialised expertise. Therefore, judicial restraint is sometimes considered appropriate where constitutional rights are not directly threatened. However, judicial restraint does not imply judicial abdication. Courts may intervene where governmental actions are arbitrary, violate constitutional guarantees, exceed legal authority, or undermine fundamental rights. The doctrine of checks and balances recognises that constitutional organs may possess limited powers to review or influence one another. Such interaction does not necessarily destroy separation of powers. For instance, executive actions may require legislative approval, legislation may be subject to constitutional scrutiny by courts, and certain appointments or actions may involve more than one branch. Constitutional governance therefore involves both separation and controlled interaction. Another important constitutional principle is the rule of law, which requires that governmental power be exercised according to established legal principles rather than personal discretion or arbitrary preference. Under the rule of law, all individuals and institutions, including public authorities, remain accountable to law. Arbitrary exercises of power are inconsistent with constitutional governance because they undermine predictability, equality, and fairness. Constitutional adjudication also frequently involves balancing majoritarian decision-making and constitutional rights. Democratic institutions ordinarily function according to majority preference. However, constitutional systems recognise that majoritarian support alone cannot justify actions violating fundamental rights. Constitutional guarantees often exist precisely to protect individuals and minority groups from excessive exercises of governmental power.

Courts may appropriately examine the law because judicial review permits scrutiny of whether legislative enactments conform to constitutional requirements, and majority support for a measure does not itself determine its constitutional validity.

The law should be upheld because democratic institutions operating according to majority preferences represent the primary source of constitutional legitimacy, and courts lack the institutional expertise to assess the national security and social stability considerations that underlie the measure.

The law raises serious constitutional concerns because requiring prior government approval of publications may implicate fundamental rights, and the passage establishes that majoritarian support alone cannot justify restrictions on rights that constitutional guarantees exist to protect.

questions.passageText: A contract of guarantee is a contract to perform the promise or discharge the liability of a third person in case of his default. It ordinarily involves three parties: the principal debtor, who is primarily liable for the debt or obligation; the creditor, to whom the obligation is owed; and the surety, who undertakes to discharge the liability if the principal debtor fails to do so. The liability of the surety is generally co- extensive with that of the principal debtor, unless otherwise provided by the contract. This means that the surety may be called upon to satisfy the same obligation that the principal debtor was bound to perform. Unlike ordinary contracts, consideration in a contract of guarantee may consist of any act, promise, or benefit done for the benefit of the principal debtor. It is not necessary that the surety receive direct consideration personally. However, a valid guarantee requires free consent, and if consent is obtained through misrepresentation or concealment of material facts, the guarantee may become invalid. For instance, if the creditor deliberately suppresses information regarding the financial condition or conduct of the principal debtor and such information would have influenced the surety's decision, the guarantee may be affected. Guarantees may be specific or continuing. A specific guarantee applies to a single transaction or obligation and comes to an end once that transaction is completed. A continuing guarantee, however, extends to a series of transactions and remains operative until revoked or otherwise terminated according to law. A continuing guarantee may be revoked by the surety concerning future transactions through notice to the creditor. However, such revocation does not affect transactions that have already occurred before the notice was given. Further, the death of a surety ordinarily operates as revocation of a continuing guarantee with respect to future transactions, unless there exists a contract providing otherwise. The law also recognises certain circumstances under which the surety may be discharged from liability. A surety may be discharged if the creditor and principal debtor enter into a contract varying the terms of the original agreement without the surety's consent, where the creditor releases the principal debtor, or where the creditor acts in a manner impairing the surety's eventual remedies against the principal debtor. Such discharge may occur because the surety agreed to guarantee only a specific obligation and should not be subjected to materially altered risks without consent. After satisfying the debt, the surety acquires certain rights against the principal debtor. This principle, often referred to as subrogation, permits the surety to step into the shoes of the creditor and exercise the rights that the creditor could have exercised against the principal debtor. The surety may also claim indemnification from the principal debtor for amounts rightfully paid under the guarantee.
options: Q is correct because consideration in a guarantee must move directly to the surety.
Q is correct because benefit to the principal debtor is legally irrelevant.
Q is incorrect because consideration benefiting the principal debtor is sufficient.
Q is incorrect because contracts of guarantee do not require consideration.

questions.questionText: P operated a tourist boating service on a river known for periodic seasonal rainfall. Weather authorities issued warnings three days in advance predicting unusually strong storms and dangerous water conditions. Despite this, P continued operations without reducing capacity or taking additional safety measures. During a severe storm, several boats overturned causing injuries to passengers. P argues that the storm was a natural occurrence and therefore an Act of God. Which of the following is most appropriate?
questions.directionsText: Directions for questions 53 to 82: You have been given some passages followed by questions based on each passage. You are required to choose the most appropriate option which follows from the passage.
questions.passageText: The law of tort recognises that a person may not always be held liable for damage merely because harm has occurred. Certain circumstances may excuse liability where the defendant demonstrates that the event occurred despite the exercise of reasonable care and caution. Two closely related yet distinct concepts in this regard are inevitable accident and Act of God (Vis Major). Although both may relieve a defendant from liability, they differ in their origin and legal requirements. An inevitable accident refers to an occurrence which could not have been prevented despite the exercise of reasonable care, caution, and skill by the defendant. The central inquiry is not whether the event caused damage, but whether a reasonable and prudent person exercising ordinary care could have avoided it. The event may arise from human conduct, mechanical failure, or unforeseen circumstances. However, the defendant cannot rely upon inevitable accident where negligence, omission, or lack of proper precautions contributed to the occurrence. Thus, a person who fails to inspect equipment, ignores warning signs, or neglects ordinary safety measures cannot later claim that the accident was inevitable. An Act of God, on the other hand, is a natural event arising exclusively from forces of nature that are so extraordinary and unforeseeable that no amount of human foresight or reasonable care could prevent the resulting damage. Examples may include unprecedented floods, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, or violent natural disturbances. The natural event must operate independently of human intervention and must be so unusual that it could not reasonably have been anticipated. Ordinary seasonal rainfall, predictable weather conditions, or recurring natural events generally do not qualify merely because they cause harm. The distinction between these principles becomes important where natural events and human conduct combine. If a natural event merely contributes to the damage but human negligence substantially contributes to the loss, liability may still arise. Conversely, where the defendant exercised reasonable care and the damage was solely attributable to an extraordinary natural force, the defence of Act of God may succeed. The burden generally lies upon the defendant to establish facts supporting these defences. Further, where a defendant voluntarily undertakes a hazardous activity or introduces potentially dangerous things into their control, courts may closely examine whether reasonable precautions proportionate to the risk were adopted.
options: P may succeed because any event involving natural forces automatically constitutes an Act of God.
P may not succeed because predictable natural conditions combined with inadequate precautions may defeat the defence.
P may succeed because negligence becomes irrelevant whenever nature contributes to harm.
P may succeed because storms and floods always constitute extraordinary events.
questions.solution: Official source answer key: Choice B.

The company records both the usual speeds and the actual speeds of vans because traffic and road conditions often affect travel time. The usual speed of the van traveling to Arvind Nagar was constant on most days. However, on Monday, due to heavy traffic, the actual speed of the van became 20% lower than its usual speed. Because of this reduction, the van took 1 hour more than usual to complete the journey. The distance to Arvind Nagar was 240 km. The distance to Bhola Town was 25% more than the distance to Arvind Nagar. The usual speed of the Bhola Town van was 25% higher than the usual speed of the Arvind Nagar van. However, on Monday, the actual speed of the Bhola Town van became 20% lower than its usual speed because of rain. The distance to Chitra City and Bhola Town were in the ratio 5 : 4. The usual speed of the Chitra City van was equal to the actual speed of the Bhola Town van. However, due to lesser traffic, the actual speed of the Chitra City van on Monday became 25% higher than its usual speed. The distance to Devgarh was 50% more than the distance to Arvind Nagar. Due to road repairs, the van to Devgarh traveled at 10% lower speed than usual on Monday and therefore reached half an hour late.

questions.questionText: What was the respective ratio of the reduction in petrol and diesel consumption by the Agriculture ministry?
questions.directionsText: Directions for questions 115 to 120: Answer the questions on the basis of the information given below.
questions.passageText: Following a national directive issued by the Prime Minister to reduce fossil fuel consumption, six ministries - Transport, Defence, Agriculture, Health, Infrastructure, and Education - implemented measures to cut down on the usage of petrol and diesel. The total petrol and diesel consumption per month of all the ministries together before the directive was 550,000 liters and 900,000 liters, respectively. The Education ministry consumed 50000 liters of petrol and the Defence ministry consumed twice that quantity whereas the ratio of petrol consumption by the Transport, Agriculture, Health, and Infrastructure ministries was 6 : 4 : 3 : 7, respectively. The Transport and Infrastructure ministries consumed 200,000 liters of diesel each whereas the ratio of diesel consumption by the Defence, Agriculture, Health, and Education ministries was 9 : 7 : 5 : 4, respectively. After taking corrective measures, there was a total reduction of 20% in the petrol consumption by all ministries. Now, the Education and Defence ministries respectively consumed 45000 liters and 85000 liters of petrol whereas the ratio of petrol consumption of the Transport, Agriculture, Health, and Infrastructure ministries became 9 : 6 : 5 : 11, respectively. Similarly there was a total reduction of 16⅔% in the diesel consumption after corrective measures were put in place. Now the Health, and Education ministries consumed 80000 and 70000 liters of diesel, respectively whereas the ratio of the diesel consumption by the Transport, Defence, Agriculture, and Infrastructure ministries became 16 : 15 : 11 : 18, respectively. The cost per litre of petrol is Rs.100 and that of diesel is Rs.90. A ministry is considered “efficient” if it reduces at least 20% of its total fuel consumption. Also, Savings = reduction in consumption × respective fuel cost
questions.solution: Official source answer key: Choice B.
